interview_metadata.name: Kennedi Terry
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Camden, New Jersey, and raised mostly around Glassboro in a pretty close South Jersey family. My parents were steady people: my dad worked in telecommunications and my mom worked in a school office, so I grew up around schedules, church, family cookouts, and a lot of talk about doing things the right way. I was the kid who liked puzzles, taking apart the family computer, and writing down steps so I could do things again. In high school I got pulled toward technology because one teacher let me help troubleshoot the computer lab, and that was the first time I thought, okay, this could be a career. I went to Rowan and finished a bachelor's in information systems, which was a big deal in my family because I was the first to get a STEM degree. After college I started on a help desk, then moved into network operations, and over time I built a career around Cisco, Juniper, cloud security, and keeping systems stable when everybody else is panicking. Personally, I have never been married and I do not have children, but I am close with my parents, my brother, my niece and nephew, and a circle of friends from church, work, tennis, and tech groups. The big themes in my life have been routine, faith, family, proving I belong in technical rooms, and still leaving space for music, photography, travel, and community work.

follow_ups.question: When you think about your childhood, what is one scene that really captures the household you grew up in?
follow_ups.response: Sunday afternoons come to mind: church in the morning, my mother checking on greens in the kitchen, my father watching football, and somebody telling a story about an auntie or grandparent that always had a lesson in it.

follow_ups.question: What were you like as a teenager?
follow_ups.response: I was responsible but a little nerdy, the one with a planner and a library card, but I also loved R&B, school dances, and going to football games with friends.

follow_ups.question: What parts of that early life still show up in your daily life now?
follow_ups.response: The routines definitely stayed: I document my work, water my garden on a schedule, meal prep on Sundays, and I still show up for family events even when work has me tired.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: One big crossroads was after college when I was working help desk and got offered a more customer-facing support supervisor track. It was safer and more predictable, and honestly people were nudging me toward it because I was good with customers. At the same time, one of the senior network engineers let me shadow during a firewall migration, and I could feel my brain lighting up in a different way. I knew taking the technical path meant more certifications, more late nights, and being one of very few Black women in those rooms. I chose networking anyway, even though it was intimidating. That choice shaped everything: my income, my confidence, my sense that I could build systems instead of just reacting to tickets.

follow_ups.question: Who helped you make that decision?
follow_ups.response: A mentor named Carla, who was a systems analyst at the hospital, told me, 'Don't let comfort pick your ceiling.' That stuck with me.

follow_ups.question: What did you have to give up by choosing the technical path?
follow_ups.response: I gave up some predictability. I had to study at night, take on-call shifts, and deal with being underestimated more than I would have liked.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was conscious. I remember sitting in my car after work with a Cisco book on the passenger seat and deciding I was going to give myself one year to really try the network track.

follow_ups.question: Did you tell anyone about that one-year plan?
follow_ups.response: I told my mother and Carla. My mother did not understand all the technical pieces, but she understood discipline and told me to write the goal down.

follow_ups.question: What was the first concrete step you took?
follow_ups.response: I signed up for a CCNA prep class, blocked out Tuesday and Thursday evenings, and started staying late to watch change windows.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. A formal mentorship program would have helped a lot, especially one for women of color in infrastructure roles. I found mentors, but it was informal and I had to be brave enough to ask.

follow_ups.question: What kind of support would have made the most difference?
follow_ups.response: Clear certification reimbursement, shadowing opportunities, and someone explaining the unwritten rules of technical career advancement.

follow_ups.question: Does that affect how you mentor people now?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. I try to be explicit with younger techs: here is the skill, here is the cert, here is how you ask for the next assignment.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am not married, I am not living with a partner, and I do not have children. My parents, Robert and Denise Terry, are still very important to me and live not too far away in South Jersey, so I see them regularly. My older brother Marcus lives in Mount Laurel with his wife and their two kids, and I am very much the auntie who shows up with books, coding toys, and sometimes too much advice. I also have an Aunt Elaine in Camden who is like a second mother in some ways. Family gatherings are usually around birthdays, church events, Juneteenth, Thanksgiving, Christmas, and sometimes Kwanzaa if my aunt is hosting. I dated someone seriously for a few years, but that ended in 2022, and right now I am not rushing into anything. My family can be in my business, but they are also my safety net.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your parents?
follow_ups.response: Usually once a week in person, often Sunday dinner or a quick weekday stop, and I talk to my mother by phone almost every other day.

follow_ups.question: What is your role in the family now?
follow_ups.response: I am the organized one. People call me for tech problems, travel planning, forms, passwords, and sometimes just to be the calm person in the room.

follow_ups.question: What do you enjoy doing with your niece and nephew?
follow_ups.response: I take them to the library, show them simple coding games, and during football season we make snacks and watch the Eagles if their parents let me steal them for a Sunday.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My sister-in-law, Dana, is part of my immediate circle too. We are close enough to text about the kids, recipes, and family logistics without needing Marcus in the middle.

follow_ups.question: Do you and Dana spend time together one-on-one?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes we get coffee or walk at the mall, mostly when she needs a break from the kids and I need sister energy.

follow_ups.question: Are there any strained family relationships?
follow_ups.response: Nothing major. Like most families, we have a few relatives who only appear when they need something, so I keep boundaries there.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friend is Tasha, a nurse I have known since high school. I also have Priya, who works in cloud engineering, and Omar, a coworker who has become a real friend because we have been through enough outages together to know each other's stress habits. There is also a small group from tennis and a women's tech meetup where I feel seen in a different way. I am not currently in a romantic relationship, but I am open to it if it does not throw my life into chaos. My friendships tend to be small but consistent: coffee, text threads, live music, walks, and showing up when somebody has a hard week.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your close friends?
follow_ups.response: Tasha maybe twice a month in person, Priya once a month, and the tennis group almost every week.

follow_ups.question: What do people usually come to you for?
follow_ups.response: They come to me when something needs sorting out: a job decision, a tech issue, a bill, or just needing someone who will listen without making it dramatic.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Glassboro, close enough to Rowan that you feel the college rhythm but far enough that my street is mostly families and older homeowners. It is a mixed area: Black families who have been here a long time, newer homeowners, students renting houses, and people commuting to Philly or Cherry Hill. I like that I can get to the library, a coffee shop, the grocery store, and my parents without making a whole production of it. My house has a small backyard where I keep herbs, tomatoes, peppers, and collards when I can get them to behave. The downside is student noise some weekends and traffic around campus events.

follow_ups.question: Who do you actually know on your block?
follow_ups.response: I know Ms. Porter next door, the retired couple across the street, and a young teacher two houses down. We look out for packages and text if something seems off.

follow_ups.question: Where do you spend time nearby?
follow_ups.response: The library, the community center, local coffee shops, the farmers market when it is running, and sometimes Rowan events if there is a speaker or concert.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe. I will walk in the early evening, but I am still aware of my surroundings, especially as a woman coming home after dark.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened that made you feel less safe?
follow_ups.response: There have been a few package thefts and some car break-ins nearby, but nothing violent close to my house.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors communicate about safety?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly by text and a neighborhood Facebook group, though I take some of those posts with a grain of salt.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is being rooted: family, familiar roads, Black community events, and enough quiet to recharge. The downside is that South Jersey can feel spread out, and for certain arts, restaurants, or tech events I still end up driving to Philly.

follow_ups.question: Have you thought about moving?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I fantasize about Philly or Collingswood, but Glassboro gives me space, affordability, and family access.

follow_ups.question: What would you improve about the area?
follow_ups.response: More reliable public transit, better late-evening food options, and more community programming that is not just tied to the university.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now I live by myself in a two-bedroom townhouse. Nobody is staying with me temporarily. My second bedroom is a guest room and office, so family can stay if needed, but most of the time it is just me, my work setup, too many camera bags, and garden supplies by the back door. I like the quiet, especially after a day of alerts and meetings.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever wish someone else lived with you?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes after a long day it would be nice to have built-in company, but overall I value the peace and control over my space.

follow_ups.question: How do you use the rooms in your home?
follow_ups.response: One bedroom is mine, the second is a home office and guest room, and the downstairs is kitchen, living room, and the place where all my plants seem to gather.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: No temporary members. It is just me as the permanent household member.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, I have lived alone for several years.

follow_ups.question: Do family members keep belongings at your place?
follow_ups.response: Just a few kid toys and spare coats for my niece and nephew, nothing that makes them household members.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: My niece and nephew might sleep over once in a while, and Tasha has crashed in the guest room after a late concert, but that is occasional.

follow_ups.question: How often do the kids stay over?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once every couple of months, usually a Friday night.

follow_ups.question: Do your parents ever stay overnight?
follow_ups.response: Not really. They live close enough to go home.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, there is no one who usually lives here and is away.

follow_ups.question: Any college students using your address?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Any family temporarily in care somewhere who normally lives with you?
follow_ups.response: No, thankfully not.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Weekdays start around 6:15. I check for overnight alerts, make coffee, water the garden if it is warm, and start work around 8:30. Mondays are usually planning and documentation, Tuesdays often have change reviews, Wednesdays I try to play tennis after work, and Thursdays are either mentoring or a family check-in. Fridays are lighter if there is no incident, so I may meet a friend or go hear live jazz. Saturdays are errands, community center tutoring, soccer when the league is in season, and photography if I can get out. Sundays are church some weeks, family dinner, meal prep, laundry, and Eagles football when it is that season.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually wear for a normal workday?
follow_ups.response: If I am remote, it is a neat top, jeans, and sneakers; if I am onsite, dark slacks, a blouse or company polo, and comfortable shoes because I may end up in a server room.

follow_ups.question: What is your Sunday meal prep like?
follow_ups.response: I usually bake chicken with smoked paprika, make greens or roasted vegetables, cook brown rice or sweet potatoes, and prep enough lunches so I do not spend money out every day.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I am a senior network and systems administrator for a regional healthcare organization in South Jersey. My normal hours are Monday through Friday, roughly 8:30 to 5:30, with hybrid days split between home and the office or data center. I manage network infrastructure, firewalls, VPNs, monitoring, server issues, cloud connectivity, and documentation. I am also on call about one week out of every five, so some evenings or weekends I may get pulled into an outage or maintenance window. I do not have a second paid job, though I volunteer and sometimes do small informal tech help for community organizations.

follow_ups.question: What does a stressful workday look like?
follow_ups.response: A stressful day is when a clinic VPN drops, a firewall rule breaks something, and three managers want updates before we even know the root cause.

follow_ups.question: What part of the job do you enjoy most?
follow_ups.response: I like designing something reliable, documenting it cleanly, and then seeing fewer emergency calls because the system is healthier.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I volunteer at a community center tutoring middle-school students in basic coding and digital literacy, usually two Saturdays a month. I also help my parents with online accounts, appointment portals, and anything that involves passwords because they trust me more than the help desk. At home I keep a garden schedule, pay bills twice a month, and try to read at least a few nights a week. Fitness-wise, I play pickup tennis weekly and casual adult soccer when the league is running, mostly for cardio and stress relief.

follow_ups.question: What do you teach the students at the community center?
follow_ups.response: We do Scratch, basic Python logic, internet safety, and sometimes simple hardware lessons so computers feel less mysterious.

follow_ups.question: What do you read when you have time?
follow_ups.response: Mystery novels and biographies of African-American leaders. I like a book with both a puzzle and some backbone.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest recent change is that I have been more intentional about health. My blood pressure crept up last year, so I added morning walks twice a week and cut back on salty takeout. Work also shifted to more cloud security projects, so I am studying for certifications again in the evenings. That has made my schedule feel tighter, but it also feels like an investment in where I want to go. I am trying not to let studying take over every joyful thing.

follow_ups.question: When do you study?
follow_ups.response: Usually Tuesday and Thursday evenings from about 7:30 to 9, after dinner and after I check work alerts.

follow_ups.question: What have you cut back on to make room?
follow_ups.response: Some streaming, some random scrolling, and a little bit of spontaneous weeknight socializing.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so I do not have a school-year routine of my own. I am involved with my niece and nephew, though. My niece does dance and my nephew is into soccer and video games, and I sometimes help with pickup or homework if Marcus and Dana are juggling work. I am not the primary caregiver, but I am part of the village.

follow_ups.question: How often do you help with them on school days?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a month, usually if a parent has a late meeting or an appointment.

follow_ups.question: What kind of homework do you help with?
follow_ups.response: Math, reading projects, and anything involving a laptop or school portal.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have not had major legal trouble, but I have had the regular experiences that make you cautious. I have been pulled over a couple of times, and even when the officer was polite, I felt my body tighten because you do not know how quickly things can turn. I have also seen police at community events, church events, and school programs, where the interaction was friendly and straightforward. So my view is mixed: I know individual officers can be decent, but I do not ignore the bigger patterns, especially for Black people.

follow_ups.question: Can you describe one traffic stop that stayed with you?
follow_ups.response: In 2017 I got stopped on Route 55 for a brake light. I had my license ready, kept my hands visible, and answered carefully even though it was supposedly routine.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever called police yourself?
follow_ups.response: Once for a car break-in on the block. They took the report, but I did not expect much beyond paperwork.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: My brother was stopped more often when he was younger, especially driving at night, and that shaped how my family talked about police. I also remember community meetings after 2020 where people were trying to speak honestly but respectfully about policing.

follow_ups.question: How did your parents talk to you and your brother about police?
follow_ups.response: They gave us the talk: be respectful, keep your hands visible, do not argue roadside, and call home as soon as you can.

follow_ups.question: Did those community meetings feel useful?
follow_ups.response: Somewhat. They created space, but I wanted more concrete policy changes and less public relations language.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. One cousin had a marijuana possession charge years ago that was later expunged, but in the moment it affected jobs and family stress more than people realized.

follow_ups.question: Did that change how your family thought about the justice system?
follow_ups.response: Yes, because it showed how one small charge could follow a young person and make everything harder.

follow_ups.question: Are you close with that cousin now?
follow_ups.response: We are friendly but not very close. I mostly see him at family events.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in almost every election, including local and school board races. My parents treated voting like a responsibility, not a hobby, so that got passed down. I usually read sample ballots, check judicial races if I can find information, and remind friends about deadlines. I have voted by mail before, but I actually like going in person when my schedule allows.

follow_ups.question: What elections do you pay the most attention to?
follow_ups.response: Presidential and congressional races get the noise, but I pay close attention to local council, school board, and county positions because they touch daily life.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever help others vote?
follow_ups.response: I remind my parents, send links to friends, and have helped older church members check registration online.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as a practical Democrat with progressive leanings, especially on civil rights, healthcare access, education, labor fairness, and voting rights. I believe government has a responsibility to keep basic systems functioning and fair, but I also care about competence and implementation because I work in systems all day. I am not impressed by slogans from either side if there is no plan behind them. Race matters in my politics because I have seen how policy shows up differently depending on your neighborhood, school, and job network. I am pro-union generally, even though my own job is not union, and I think working people need more stability. On public safety, I want accountability and prevention, not just more force. I would say I am left of center but not someone who wants chaos for the sake of change.

follow_ups.question: What issues would most influence your vote right now?
follow_ups.response: Healthcare costs, voting rights, racial equity, cybersecurity and infrastructure, abortion rights, and whether a candidate seems serious about governing.

follow_ups.question: Are there any views where you are more moderate?
follow_ups.response: I am pretty pragmatic on budgets and public administration. I want programs funded, but I also want them measured and run well.

follow_ups.question: Do your tech background and politics connect?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Cybersecurity, broadband access, privacy, and digital literacy are political issues to me because they determine who can participate safely and fully.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more local in my thinking. I used to focus mostly on national elections, but the pandemic, policing debates, school board fights, and housing pressure made me pay closer attention to county and municipal decisions. I have also become more concerned about misinformation because I see how fast bad information spreads online, including in family group chats. I would not say my values changed, but my sense of where power operates has changed. I am more likely now to ask, who is actually implementing this and who is being left out?

follow_ups.question: What made misinformation feel more personal?
follow_ups.response: Seeing relatives share bad vaccine information and then seeing the same pattern with elections and crime stories made it feel close to home.

follow_ups.question: Have you attended any local meetings?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a couple school board and community safety meetings, plus Juneteenth planning meetings where local officials showed up.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They affected me a lot, though not because the issues were new to me. What changed was how public and unavoidable the conversation became, especially after George Floyd. I remember feeling grief, anger, and exhaustion, but also a strange relief that some people who had ignored these conversations finally had to hear them. At work, it made me more willing to speak up when diversity conversations stayed too vague. In family life, it brought up stories from older relatives that I had heard before but understood differently as an adult.

follow_ups.question: Did you participate in any public response?
follow_ups.response: I attended a local vigil and one peaceful march, and I joined a few workplace listening sessions.

follow_ups.question: Did it change relationships with coworkers?
follow_ups.response: With some people it deepened trust. With others, I learned who wanted to move past discomfort without understanding it.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think about them as bigger than one organization or slogan. To me the issues are about whether Black life is treated as fully human in schools, healthcare, housing, employment, and policing. I care about police accountability, but I also care about the upstream things: mental health resources, youth programs, job access, and whether communities have a voice in budgets. I do not believe every problem gets solved by one reform. But I do believe ignoring the racial pattern is dishonest.

follow_ups.question: What would meaningful change look like to you?
follow_ups.response: Transparent discipline data, better crisis response, less tolerance for misconduct, and real investment in youth and neighborhood resources.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about this with younger people you mentor?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but carefully. I want them informed and proud, not scared all the time.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I have been thinking about how race keeps showing up in systems even when people insist they are only talking about something else. It shows up in whose schools get resources, whose pain gets believed, whose neighborhoods get investment, and who gets assumed competent at work. As a Black woman in tech, I also think about representation and the extra performance of calmness that gets expected from us. At the same time, I do not want my whole life narrated through struggle. There is joy, culture, humor, music, food, and community too.

follow_ups.question: Where do you feel race most in your own daily life?
follow_ups.response: At work when I am the only Black woman in a technical meeting, and in public situations where I am aware of being read before I even speak.

follow_ups.question: Where do you feel racial identity as strength?
follow_ups.response: In family gatherings, church, music, storytelling, Juneteenth events, and mentoring younger Black women in tech.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with family and friends, attended a vigil and a peaceful march, donated to a bail fund once, and pushed for more concrete mentorship and hiring discussions at work. I am not out every weekend protesting, but I am not silent either.

follow_ups.question: Where do you feel most comfortable speaking up?
follow_ups.response: Small groups, workplace committees, and mentoring spaces. I am better in a focused conversation than yelling into the internet.

follow_ups.question: Have you lost relationships over these conversations?
follow_ups.response: Not lost, but I have pulled back from a few acquaintances who kept treating racism like a debate exercise.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My parents were sad but not surprised; they have lived enough to recognize the pattern. My brother was angry, especially thinking about his own traffic stops and his son growing up. My friends mostly wanted action, but we handled it differently: some protested more, some donated, some focused on workplace equity, and some just needed breaks from the news. In my circle there was also a lot of checking on each other emotionally.

follow_ups.question: Did your family discuss it with the children?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but age-appropriately. My brother and Dana talked about fairness, safety, and pride without putting adult fear fully on them.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone close to you disagree strongly?
follow_ups.response: A couple extended relatives are more conservative, but even they understood the fear around traffic stops.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I would say my health is good, but I am more aware at 40 that I have to maintain it. I have mild hypertension that I am managing with medication, walking, and cutting back on sodium. I also have seasonal allergies and the occasional desk-worker back and neck stiffness. Tennis and soccer help, but they also remind me I am not 25 anymore. Mentally, I am mostly steady, though work stress can show up as tension and trouble sleeping.

follow_ups.question: What medication do you take for blood pressure?
follow_ups.response: A low dose of amlodipine, plus regular check-ins with my primary care doctor.

follow_ups.question: How do you track your health?
follow_ups.response: I use a home blood pressure cuff a few mornings a week and track steps on my watch, though I am not obsessive about it.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Routine makes it easier. If I meal prep, schedule tennis, and keep healthy food in the house, I do pretty well. What makes it hard is on-call work, late incidents, family events with rich food, and stress cravings for salty snacks. South Jersey driving culture does not help either because you can end up sitting a lot. I do better when health is built into the week instead of treated like a separate project.

follow_ups.question: What healthy foods do you actually enjoy?
follow_ups.response: Roasted sweet potatoes, collards with garlic and apple cider vinegar, baked chicken, fresh herbs, berries, and a good salad if it has enough texture.

follow_ups.question: What is your hardest habit to manage?
follow_ups.response: Late-night snacking when I am doing maintenance windows or studying.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: The main thing was the hypertension diagnosis in 2025. It was not a crisis, but my doctor was clear that family history plus stress meant I needed to take it seriously. I also had some knee tendinitis after overdoing soccer and tennis in the same week, so I did physical therapy exercises and bought better shoes. No broken bones or major surgeries. It was more of a wake-up call than a dramatic event.

follow_ups.question: How did you react to the hypertension diagnosis?
follow_ups.response: I was annoyed at first because I thought I was doing okay, but then I got practical and treated it like a system needing maintenance.

follow_ups.question: Did the knee issue stop you from sports?
follow_ups.response: For a few weeks, yes. Now I stretch more and do not stack soccer and tennis too aggressively.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not stopped me from working. The closest is when stress or lack of sleep after an outage makes me less patient the next day, but I manage it with rest, walking, and taking PTO when I need to.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever needed accommodations at work?
follow_ups.response: No formal accommodations, just normal flexibility to work from home after late maintenance if my manager approves.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry health could affect work later?
follow_ups.response: A little, which is why I am trying to handle the blood pressure now instead of pretending it is nothing.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My father worked as a telecommunications technician. follow_ups.question: Did his work influence your career?

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?

The company maintained communication infrastructure, handled installations and repairs, and supported customers when service went down. In our house, that meant I understood early that invisible systems matter.

follow_ups.question: Was it union work?
follow_ups.response: Parts of that industry were unionized, and he respected what unions did for working people.

follow_ups.question: Did he talk about work at home?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, usually as a lesson about preparation, safety, or not cutting corners.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope to be in a senior leadership role like network architect, cybersecurity manager, or IT operations director. I want my CCNP and CISSP finished, and I want to lead teams that build security and maintenance into everyday habits instead of treating them like emergencies. I also want to launch a mentorship program for Black women in technology in South Jersey, something practical with resume reviews, lab nights, speakers, and real job pathways. Personally, I hope my parents stay healthy, my home feels settled, and I have room for love if the right relationship comes along. I want to take the Ghana trip, keep photographing cities and parks, and maybe eventually build a boutique consulting firm for small businesses that need reliable network and security help. I want growth, but not at the cost of peace.

follow_ups.question: What is the first step toward that future?
follow_ups.response: Finish the CCNP track, then map out CISSP study and ask for more architecture responsibility at work.

follow_ups.question: What would the mentorship program look like in practice?
follow_ups.response: Monthly sessions, hands-on labs, guest speakers, certification study groups, and matching early-career women with working professionals.

follow_ups.question: What kind of travel do you hope for?
follow_ups.response: Mostly cultural trips: Ghana for ancestry and history, New Orleans for jazz, Savannah for architecture, and weekend museum trips to Philly or D.C.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value family, integrity, stability, community, faith, and the ability to keep learning. I value being reliable, but I am also learning not to confuse reliability with carrying everything alone. I value Black culture and the stories that kept my family grounded. I value good work done with care, whether that is a secure network, a pan of collards, or showing a student that technology is not out of reach. And I value joy: music, laughter, a good book, a clean kitchen, and a Sunday when nobody calls me about a firewall.

follow_ups.question: Which value guides your decisions most often?
follow_ups.response: Integrity. If I cannot explain the choice honestly, I probably should not be making it.

follow_ups.question: What do you want people to say about you?
follow_ups.response: That I showed up, did the work well, made room for others, and still had some music in my life.
